evidence.fact: Axon Draft One already writes draft incident reports from body-cam audio and saves roughly 40% of report-writing time. Officers still have to attest to each report, and it then goes through sergeant review and records review.

At Arvada PD, officers review, edit and finalize every AI-drafted report, and supervisors review and approve all submitted reports. The AI is treated as a support tool, and humans remain responsible for accuracy.

California SB 524 (Penal Code 13663, in effect since 1 January 2026) requires AI-assisted police reports to carry a disclosure and an officer's signature confirming the facts, and the first AI draft must be kept.

Existing AI returns agents check the order, test eligibility against written policy, work out the refund or store credit and update the order and payment systems. Policy exceptions are escalated to a human, so they still need human judgment.

Retail planning software already uses AI to split top-level open-to-buy budgets across product and location groups and to adjust replenishment automatically. Logile markets AI-built store labor budgets.

In-store refund and void approvals rely on manager overrides tied to named user accounts. Loss-prevention experts recommend a second approval for higher-value refunds. This is an internal control set by each retailer, not a legal or licensing requirement, and approvals can already be done remotely from a mobile device.

PackageX Mailroom says its AI and machine vision read package labels from a photo, match items to recipients, send email, SMS or WhatsApp alerts and record proof of pickup. This automates the logging and notification steps, though the claims come from the vendor's own materials.
The app lets staff batch-scan packages and notify all recipients with one tap. A person still has to physically receive, scan, sort and hand over the items.

Independent reviews mostly repeat the vendor's description. Vendors pitch self-service workflows as a way to reduce front-desk work, not as autonomous handling of physical mail, which an agent without a body cannot do.

Operto ONE runs seven AI agents across front-of-house and back-of-house hotel work. A supervisory layer decides whether each agent drafts, recommends or acts, depending on how confident it is. The agents coordinate tasks, but managers still oversee them.

Apaleo and THE FLAG run an agentic AI in live hotel operations that creates tasks for departments on its own, such as extra beds or cots. It saves about 3.5 hours a week of task creation. It routes and coordinates operational work but does not replace managers conferring with each other.

Sirma's Marta agent links to the PMS, revenue and operations systems. It updates plans and sends tasks to the right teams, which covers the information-sharing part of coordination. Decisions and negotiation between managers stay with humans.

AI needs-assessment generators can build a framework that pulls together census and demographic data, service utilization records, survey instruments and engagement strategies. They produce plans and templates, not finished analyses of the data.

A 2026 academic paper describes using AI for pattern detection, classification, prioritization and decision support on community-needs survey data to guide program planning. This shows the analysis sub-steps can be automated, though it is a research method rather than a deployed product.

Census figures are the standard population source for needs assessments but do not give an exact count of a community. Program needs assessments still rely on direct input from community members, which calls for human engagement and judgment to interpret.

Vendors sell purchase-order tracking agents. These agents read open PO records, supplier emails, receipts and invoices, label the status of each order and draft chase notes for a buyer to review. A human review step is still built in.
Dynamics 365 ERP MCP servers let AI agents reach live ERP purchasing and inventory data directly. Other vendor agents connect to SAP, Oracle and NetSuite and log every PO action for audit.

Supplier performance agents pull delivery, quality and cost data from ERP records and score suppliers against targets automatically. Vendors still stress human approval for important supplier decisions.

Vendor material describes ITAM, procurement and MDM pipelines (an HRIS trigger, then an asset request, then Jamf/Intune enrollment) that automate the digital side: reading orders, matching the hardware to the role, and setting up the device. Each new hire automatically triggers an asset request in the ITAM platform.

In zero-touch deployment, devices ship from the vendor already configured, which cuts down the technician's hands-on setup. Physical checks and handling still happen at the vendor or depot. The agent has no body, so it cannot look over the hardware itself.
IT provisioning and asset roles still involve hands-on prep and inspection of hardware before it is handed to users. No law or licence requires a human to sign off on this.

Oracle Autonomous Database and Data Safe already automate routine security work: security patching (Oracle says without downtime), encryption, user and security assessments, activity monitoring and data masking. Customers still have to classify their data and check that access policies match their rules.
Oracle says its autonomous database applies security patches automatically and encrypts network traffic automatically. Both claims come from Oracle's own materials.

Agents with database access can change permissions, and reported incidents include an agent running a destructive query on a production database. Guidance therefore calls for least-privilege access and human oversight, so a human still has to review and approve security changes before they are used.

Sketch-to-CAD and drawing-to-CAD AI tools in 2026 handle simple geometry from digital sketches or images. Complex parts still need human cleanup, and engineers review and approve the output. These tools help digitally but do not draw sketches by hand, trace onto paper or run copiers.

Turiya AI reads drawings supplied as images or PDFs and generates CAD code and 3D models. Engineers stay in control and review the results, so the tool supports digital reproduction steps rather than physical tracing or copying.
Drafter certification (ADDA Certified Drafter) is voluntary, and no general license is needed to draft, trace or reproduce drawings.
Library systems already let patrons pay fines online through PayPal or card. Payments post to the patron's account automatically, so collection needs no staff action.
Patrons can choose which fines to pay and pay part of a fine through self-service online portals.
Library chatbots answer routine fine and account questions. Judgment calls, such as disputes or waivers, still go to a human, and in-person cash payments at the desk need someone physically there.

Pharmacy inventory software already handles the main record-keeping steps. It automatically reconciles wholesaler invoices so staff don't have to match paper invoices against packing slips by hand, and it keeps purchase orders and inventory levels up to date. An agent working in the browser could run these screens from start to finish.

Pharmacy management systems update a running inventory count from electronic wholesaler data (EDI) and invoices, and can track stock by lot and expiry date. Most of the data entry is structured digital work that an agent can do.

For controlled substances, the buyer has to record how many containers actually arrived and the date they arrived. Someone has to physically count the delivery, and only an authorized registrant can sign Form 222 or use a CSOS certificate. This keeps a human involved for checking deliveries and for the controlled-substance steps, even though the aide's routine record entry doesn't require a licence.

Jail management systems already handle booking records, charges, bond and holds, and they auto-fill arrest and charge data from connected CAD/RMS or arrest-report systems. This automates much of the data entry and updating.
Arrest information can be pulled into the jail system to fill in cases, charges and bond details, and staff can update charges, court dates and inmate records in real time.

Identification needs in-person steps by corrections deputies: Live Scan fingerprinting, photos, and documenting scars and tattoos. Checking identity against NCIC and state databases happens inside restricted criminal-justice (CJIS) systems.

Machines that peel produce automatically, such as the Minerva Omega onion and potato peeler at up to 240 kg/h, are mechanical kitchen equipment. They are not software AI agents, so the reference technology, which has no body, cannot run or replace them.
Peeling machines sold to restaurants, like the Cancan 1323, still need a person to load, run and unload them. Washing, peeling, cutting and seeding produce all means handling it physically.

Commercial vegetable prep machines such as the IMC MF5 are electromechanical tools. The task is manual or machine-assisted work, so an agent that only uses software can do nothing meaningful here beyond things like recipe or cut-spec lookup.
Automated meat cutting depends on physical robots: a six-axis arm with 3-D machine vision is used to cut beef hocks in processing plants. That is industrial robotics, not a software agent.
Research systems that cut pork carcasses into primal cuts need fixtures, saws and robot arms. The task is physical manipulation of the meat.
Fully automatic primal cutting of pig half carcasses uses a vision-positioned saw. This is specialised hardware that a software-only agent cannot operate in a typical kitchen.

The robots that help with bussing (Bear Robotics Servi, Pizza Ranch units) are physical carts. Humans still load the dirty dishes, and the robots carry them to the dish room. That makes them robotics, not software agents, and they still don't wipe tables.
Even a purpose-built autonomous bussing robot (Smile Robotics) is much slower than a human at clearing tables. This shows the task depends on physical manipulation.
Restaurants deploy robots to carry dirty dishes to the dish room, which is entirely physical work. An agent that acts only through software has nothing to act on.
Caring for Our Children defines cleaning as physically removing dirt with soap, water and friction, then sanitizing surfaces. This is hands-on handling of objects.
Childcare guidance says mouthed and shared toys must be cleaned and sanitized at least daily or whenever soiled. Some guidance says after each use, with a separate bin for mouthed toys.
Sanitizers must be EPA-registered and used as the label says, including dilution and contact time. Licensing sets the standards but does not require a licensed person to do the cleaning.

ChatCPR is an open-source AI tool from UC San Diego, Johns Hopkins and UPMC. It talks bystanders through CPR and did better than human 911 dispatchers in early testing (May 2026). This is help to a human who does the CPR, not a replacement, so it supports L1 at most.
A test with 21 people used a voice chatbot to guide untrained users through CPR. Only 33% of them gave high-quality CPR. In every case a human had to do the chest compressions with their own hands.
Most states require child-care providers to hold first aid and CPR certification. This is a training rule for the caregiver, and it assumes a person on the spot gives the care by hand.

Camera and IoT baby monitors (for example CuboAi, and research prototypes such as ThermoCam) can watch a child and send fever or temperature alerts. They support observation, but they do not take a reading by hand, drive a child to the doctor or give medicine.

Under Texas HB 1615 (Nathan's Law), child-care staff need a parent's signed, electronic or phoned-in authorization before giving a child medication. The rule covers medication given through a parent's authorization; it does not require a licensed professional, so a lay caregiver can do it with consent.
Utah's child-care rules require parental consent each time over-the-counter medication is given. Giving medication is a physical, hands-on job done by the caregiver who is present.

Park and recreation departments already use AI to draft social media posts and program descriptions, and to suggest new programs from national trend data and local data. This covers the promote and organize sub-steps.

Rec Technologies sells recreation management software it calls AI-powered, with email and SMS program marketing and help with registration and administration. Its feature claims come from its own vendor pages.
Recreation workers plan and lead activities in person, supervise participants and keep them safe. Some employers require CPR or first aid certification, so the leading part needs physical presence.

Vendor pages say AI property-inquiry assistants answer buyer questions around the clock. They cover property details, HOA fees, taxes and mortgage estimates, and they qualify buyers on financing. These are marketing claims with no independent accuracy data.
A mortgage AI tool (Roof AI from Mortgageable) answers routine financing questions 24/7 and sends complex cases to human advisers. This supports partial delegation, not full delegation.

Agents who answer outside their expertise, such as repair costs, construction or inspections, face negligence claims and discipline. That gives a reason to have a human review answers, though no law says a human must give them. These sources are secondary.

Libraries now automate returns sorting with robotic materials handling: conveyors read each item's RFID tag and route it to bins. That is physical robotics, which is outside the reference agent's abilities.
Even with automated sorters, staff still carry materials to the shelves on carts and place them by hand. Shelving remains physical work.
Sorting is driven by RFID lookups in the library management system (SIP2). That digital step is small and already automated, and no law requires a human to do or sign this task.

Aurelian's AI voice assistant is used by more than a dozen 911 centers, including Snohomish County WA, Chattanooga and Kalamazoo. It handles non-emergency calls such as noise and parking complaints and transfers real emergencies to a human dispatcher.
In 2025 Dakota County, MN's AI attendant redirected about 33% of calls to the dispatch center and answered common questions. Anoka County, MN is launching an AI non-emergency call taker.

AI only rarely answers 911 calls directly. NENA's operations and standards VP said a caller reporting an emergency should hear a human voice. State rules such as Utah's require at least two telecommunicators answering 911 at all times.

The carrier Hirschbach uses Augment's AI agent, Augie, for outbound driver outreach: information requests and pickup and delivery arrivals. That is about 40% of its track-and-trace contacts. Humans still handle the rest.

Vendor voice AI agents (Bubba AI, Bland, Telnyx) say they handle check calls, status updates, dispatch instructions and rescheduling. They connect to TMS and ELD systems and pass exceptions to human dispatchers. These are the vendors' own unverified claims.

A third-party guide summarizing FCC rules says business and industrial two-way land mobile radio needs no commercial operator licence. I did not confirm this against current 47 CFR Part 90, so no legal rule appears to require a human operator.
O*NET lists this as a Machinists (51-4041.00) task. The neighbouring tasks are taking machines apart with hand or power tools and replacing defective parts, which is hands-on mechanical work.

Job postings describe installing machined replacement or repaired parts in mechanisms, machines and equipment, then running the unit to check that it works. All of this needs someone physically there. An agent with no body can only help at the edges, for example by finding manuals, torque specs or installation steps.
Machinists generally do not need a licence or sign-off for this work, so the main barrier is physical, not legal.

Driverless parking at SAE Level 4 depends on specially equipped vehicles and garage infrastructure, such as the Bosch/Mercedes system approved for Stuttgart Airport's P6 garage. That is robotics and vehicle automation, not a software-only AI agent.
Parking and retrieving cars means physically driving customers' vehicles, and an agent without a body cannot do this.
City codes such as Baltimore's require each valet attendant to hold a valid driver's license and be at least 18.

Bridgit's construction workforce-planning AI agents put together project teams, find available workers and suggest assignments, but planners review and approve the suggestions before any change is made.

Sir Robert McAlpine is rolling out AI workforce-planning software across its UK operations to replace spreadsheet processes. The software checks workers' availability, certifications, location and project experience, and forecasts labour needs.
Lumber's SmartPlanner automatically picks crews by availability, skills and proximity for construction scheduling and dispatch.
AI interviewer tools run parallel one-on-one stakeholder interviews and synthesize where stakeholders agree and disagree. This supports delegating question design, conversation and synthesis.

BA practice guidance in 2026 says AI can draft requirements, but a skilled analyst is still needed to tell whether the real problem matches what the stakeholder described. The human keeps final ownership of the requirements.
In the US, no licence is needed to work as a computer systems analyst, so no legal sign-off barrier applies.

Vendor and analyst comparison guides for software platforms are widely published online in 2026, so an agent that can browse can gather and synthesize this material end to end. These guides note vendor bias and the need to verify pricing and vendor viability, which supports keeping a human review step.

Structured product assessments profile enterprise vendors (AWS, Microsoft, Google, Salesforce, ServiceNow and others) on features and roadmap. This is the kind of evidence an agent can collect and compare to draft a recommendation without a human doing each step.

Procurement guidance says to judge vendors on performance, governance, ROI and roadmap fit rather than feature checklists. That depends on internal requirements, budgets and existing systems, which usually sit with people and internal systems an agent may not reach. No licence or legal sign-off is typically required, but a human usually approves the purchase.

Vendors describe AI agents that run the maintenance paperwork from start to finish. They flag equipment anomalies, open CMMS work orders, order parts through the ERP, schedule technicians and draft service reports. These claims are self-reported, and no independently verified oilfield deployment was found.

Oil and gas work-order creation and maintenance scheduling are being automated. Manual creation reportedly takes 15–45 minutes per order, and the same pipeline is used in refinery and oilfield settings.

Under OSHA 1910.119(i), the employer must carry out a pre-startup safety review for new or modified facilities. A multi-disciplinary team of engineers, operations, maintenance and safety staff checks physically that installed equipment matches the design. This means humans have to be on site and accountable for installation and startup.

Electronic field-data and logbook tools such as MonitorPro MP-Field, SUEZ eRIS-LOG and Ambisis already handle digital entry, validation, audit trails and AI extraction of data from documents. An agent could do the record-keeping and file-maintenance steps end to end.

EPA Region 4 logbook procedure: entries must be contemporaneous, objective and legible. Hardcopy logbooks are bound and handwritten, and electronic entries need an audit trail. The observations come from the person in the field, so a human must supply or check the content.

Field logbooks are treated as accountable documents in enforcement proceedings, and the person responsible signs, dates and initials the entries. This comes from SOPs and QA plans, not from a licence requirement.

Computrition's AMPS add-on builds menus from a master menu, handling therapeutic diets and recipe substitutions. Vendors such as MealSuite and Menutech advertise automated or AI menu and nutrition planning for healthcare.

Nutrition and dietetics technicians plan menus with registered dietitian nutritionists for people with special nutritional needs. In clinical care they typically work under RDN supervision, so a human professional reviews the work.
A Brazilian school-menu tool generates weekly menus that meet nutritional references, but a nutritionist still chooses the final menu, so a human stays in the loop.

FDA-cleared home wearables such as Current Health and Mindray mWear automatically measure pulse, respiration and temperature and use software to flag changes. Software can then read, log and flag the data, but a person still has to put on, apply or operate the sensor at the patient's side.

In an Oxford hospital-at-home study, patients' own manual temperature readings were logged on only 51-58% of days, while the chest patch captured pulse and breathing rate much more consistently. Measurement still depends on someone being physically there.

Taking temperature, pulse and respiration is a standard aide skill, done non-invasively under RN supervision and reported to the supervisor. No licence requires a human to sign it, but it is a hands-on bedside task.

Vendors sell AI video analytics for casino surveillance. They say it flags dealer errors, odd hand movements, chip placement problems and suspicious betting, links play data with dealer rosters to spot collusion, and checks thousands of cameras automatically for scene compliance with regulations. These are vendor claims and have not been independently verified.

Nevada's surveillance standards set required camera coverage for games, the cage and count rooms. Only surveillance personnel and key employees may enter the surveillance room. The work is done through camera systems from a separate room rather than by handling things on the floor.

Surveillance agents must know the department's procedures, Gaming Commission regulations and minimum internal control standards. Under these rules, surveillance personnel are regulated staff with restricted access. The searches did not confirm the exact licensing requirements for these staff.

Michigan requires a case report for every body. It must list the personal effects that come with the decedent, the embalming details, and the name, license number and signature of each licensee who did the embalming. It must be kept at least 7 years.
Virginia requires a separate report for each embalming, with the embalmer's name, signature and license number, plus the supervisor's signature if an intern did the work.

Funeral home software already handles case management from first call to disposition, regulatory paperwork tracking and inventory. An agent could automate record entry and upkeep, but a person still has to look at and handle the clothing and valuables to list them.

Funeral home software such as MorTrack and Last Rites handles dispatch, vehicle tracking and allocating staff and vehicles. That covers only the planning paperwork around a procession, not the physical work.

State procession laws (Delaware, Kansas, New Hampshire) govern escort or lead vehicles driven by funeral home staff or police. Organizing a procession means a person on site driving and directing traffic.

The Tribute Technology 'Procession' product supports case and task management, so an agent could help with scheduling and notifying families. Placing the casket and leading the cortege still need a person there.

AI cameras at fixed sites can flag visitors who get too close to exhibits or cross set lines and alert a control room. Operators can then speak to visitors through two-way audio. This only covers fixed, camera-equipped venues, not moving tour groups, and the source is a vendor case study.
Tour guides are responsible for the group's safety and for keeping the group together. They watch visitors on the spot to make sure tour rules and safety practices are followed.

South Africa's Tourism Act requires registered tourist guides to take all reasonable steps to ensure the safety of the tourists they accompany. This puts a duty of care on a human guide in at least some jurisdictions. Australian training material says no licence applies to the guiding unit, so this varies by country.
HashMicro's AI agent records order requests, checks the details and creates sales orders with no manual admin work. It can also pull order data out of POs, PDFs and voice messages.
Jotform's AI Order Taker answers phone calls around the clock, collects order details and checks them in real time against existing form systems, so no staff member is needed.
Some AI ordering setups still have a human confirm orders or step in on complex or unclear cases. Accuracy depends on audio quality and how complex the menu or catalog is.

Employer and O*NET-style task descriptions say helpers thread conduit ends with a pipe threader, connect couplings and fittings with a wrench, and fabricate support brackets from strap iron with a hacksaw, shaping dies, hammer and punch, then bolt or screw the brackets in place. This is entirely physical manipulation on site.
In Maine, helper electricians are licensed and may make electrical installations only under the direct supervision of a master, journeyman or limited electrician.
In Hawaii, unlicensed helpers may do electrical work only under a licensed journey worker or supervising electrician, who must be physically present at the project site.

The O*NET task list for Helpers--Electricians (47-3013.00) describes this duty as physically raising, lowering or positioning equipment, tools and materials with a hoist, hand line or block and tackle. It sits alongside related physical duties such as rigging scaffolds, hoists and shoring.

OSHA requires a qualified rigger, meaning a person the employer judges qualified, when workers in the fall zone hook, unhook or guide a load (29 CFR 1926.1425(c)). It also requires one for hoisting during crane assembly and disassembly work (1926.1404(r)(1)).
Under OSHA, the employer decides whether a rigger is qualified, based on their knowledge, training and experience. For hoisting equipment rated at 2,000 lbs or less, a separate exception applies.

The MUTCD's automated flagger assistance devices (AFADs) still need a human flagger to run them remotely, either at one end of the work zone or from a central location. Flagging is not done autonomously by software.
Iowa's AFAD guidance requires trained flaggers on site who can switch to manual flagging if a device fails. Physical presence is needed.

State specifications require AFAD units to be linked and controlled by wireless communications with fail-safe behaviour. The devices are physical roadside hardware operated by people, not something a software agent would normally reach.

Clean-in-place (CIP) systems automate washing of pipes, vessels, tanks and fittings. They run on PLC/HMI controllers, not software AI agents, and people still have to clean the outside of equipment and the cooking area.

Automated CIP cycles push a pre-rinse, a caustic or acid wash and a post-rinse through equipment that is already in place. Hosing down, scrubbing and sanitizing the cooking area are still physical jobs done by hand.

CIP replaces a slow, hands-on routine of taking equipment apart and cleaning it by hand. That routine is physical work an agent with no body cannot do. At most it could start a CIP cycle that is already set up or log sanitation records.

Lifeguards already log weather, tides, water conditions, equipment checks and first-aid or rescue records on digital forms and apps such as SafetyCulture, SLSQ's LIMSOC and the SLSA Operations App. An agent could pre-fill the conditions data and turn a lifeguard's notes into structured reports.

Some regulators and governing bodies require signed and dated incident reports filed within set deadlines, for example Vermont's tramway incident form and New Hampshire's 5-day injury report. This makes a human who saw the event responsible for the content.

Alpine Canada's incident form must have all applicable sections completed and carries a signature and date block. Those details come from someone who was there and observed the injury and the treatment.
Robots that stir and pour pancake batter exist only as research prototypes that need robot hardware. A software-only AI agent cannot do this physical work.

Automated pancake makers are dedicated machines that dispense and cook batter, and the patent says pancake production is still mostly manual and labor-intensive. Physical handling is central to the task.
Commercial units like POPCAKE use pre-mixed batter bags in dedicated appliances. That is not something an AI agent working through software, documents or messages can do.

Commercial vivarium systems such as Setra and Rewire Neuroscience's Degrees of Freedom offer networked temperature and humidity monitoring with remote dashboards, mobile alerts and some control features. An agent with access could read data and possibly change setpoints, but these systems mostly monitor rather than adjust room conditions.

Remote control of vivarium devices through a web browser or phone app exists only in patents and research or hobbyist prototypes. Most caretakers in kennels, zoos, nurseries and farms adjust thermostats, heaters, humidifiers and vents by hand on site.

The Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and institutional policies require species-appropriate ranges, daily recorded checks and calibrated devices. They also note that conditions inside cages can differ from room readings, so on-site checking matters, but no law says a licensed human must make the adjustment.
